intro: A linear transformation is a rule that moves vectors around while keeping straight lines straight, such as a rotation or a stretch. This branch shows that every such rule can be captured by a matrix.

VII.5.01.what: A linear transformation is a function on vectors that respects adding and scaling. Rotating a picture is an example.

levels.a: Checks that transforming a sum equals the sum of the transformed parts.
levels.b: Checks that scaling before or after transforming gives the same result.
levels.c: Tests whether a given rule is linear.
levels.d: Uses the fact that a linear map always sends zero to zero.

VII.5.02.what: Every linear transformation of ordinary space can be written as a matrix, found by seeing where the basic directions go.

levels.a: Finds where the basic unit arrows are sent.
levels.b: Builds the matrix from those images.
levels.c: Applies the matrix to transform any vector.
levels.d: Understands that every such linear map comes from a matrix.

VII.5.03.what: Familiar geometric moves such as turning, mirroring and slanting are all linear transformations with simple matrices.

levels.a: Writes and uses matrices for rotations.
levels.b: Writes and uses matrices for reflections in a line.
levels.c: Writes matrices for shears (slants) and stretches.
levels.d: Writes matrices that project vectors flat onto a line.

VII.5.04.what: The kernel is everything a transformation squashes to zero; the range is everything it can reach.

levels.a: Identifies the kernel with the matrix's null space.
levels.b: Identifies the range with the matrix's column space.
levels.d: Finds their dimensions and relates them.

VII.5.05.what: A map is one-to-one if different inputs never land in the same place, and onto if every possible output is reached.

levels.a: Tests one-to-one by checking only zero goes to zero.
levels.b: Tests onto by checking the range fills the whole space.
levels.c: Uses pivot positions to test both quickly.
levels.d: Sees that a map with both properties can be undone.

VII.5.06.what: Composition means doing one transformation and then another, which matches multiplying their matrices.

levels.a: Applies one map and then a second.
levels.b: Finds the combined matrix by multiplying.
levels.c: Gets the order of multiplication right, since it matters.
levels.d: Combines geometric moves, such as a rotation then a reflection.

VII.5.07.what: An inverse transformation undoes the original, like rotating back the other way.

levels.a: Describes the map that undoes a given one.
levels.b: Finds it using the inverse matrix.
levels.d: Describes inverses of geometric moves, such as undoing a shear.

VII.5.08.what: Linear maps also act on polynomials and functions. Taking a derivative is itself a linear transformation.

levels.a: Sees taking the derivative as a linear map.
levels.b: Represents such a map by a matrix once bases are chosen.
levels.c: Computes that matrix for a given map.
levels.d: Sees integration as a linear map too.

VII.5.09.what: Similar matrices describe the same transformation seen through different coordinate systems.

levels.a: Recognizes the change-of-basis sandwich that makes matrices similar.
levels.b: Explains it as one map described in two bases.
levels.c: Lists properties that similar matrices share.
levels.d: Chooses a basis that makes the matrix especially simple.
